title: The Betrothed
author: Alessandro Manzoni
quoteNote: Quotations are from the anonymous English translation published by Richard Bentley, London, 1834 - the only complete Betrothed in the public domain, and a translation of Manzoni's first version of 1827 rather than his revised text of 1842. It condenses, and it Anglicises: Lucia is "Lucy", Fra Cristoforo is "Father Christopher", l'Innominato is "the Unknown". The map shows the Italian names a reader will meet anywhere else and records the translation's own beside them. Chapter numbers throughout are this translation's 1-37, which run one behind the Italian's 38 after chapter 27.
overture: A village priest is threatened into refusing a wedding, and the two people who were to be married spend two years and four hundred miles getting back to the morning they were interrupted. She is carried off to a castle; he walks into a bread riot in Milan and out of it with a warrant on his head, and crosses a river at dawn into another country. Then an army comes down out of the Alps carrying plague, and the map fills with a third thing that is not looking for either of them.

frontiers.name: the Duchy of Milan / the Republic of Venice
frontiers.label: MILAN · VENICE
frontiers.note: Spanish Milan ended and Venetian territory began at the Adda. Manzoni makes it load-bearing twice: Renzo has 'often heard that at a certain point, and for some distance, its waters marked the confines of the Milanese and Venetian states' (ch. 16), and the valley under the Innominato's castle carries 'a small brook, or a large torrent, which served for a boundary between the two territories' (ch. 20). Crossing it is what puts Renzo out of the law's reach for two years.
frontiers.source: The line follows the Adda from Lake Como to below Trezzo, the frontier fixed between the Duchy of Milan and the Republic of Venice and unchanged through the seventeenth century. Drawn from the river's own course; the novel names it as the border twice.

sources: Text: Project Gutenberg #35155, the anonymous English translation, Richard Bentley, London 1834, of Manzoni's 1827 first version. 37 chapters where the Italian has 38.

THE VILLAGE IS NEVER NAMED. Manzoni gives its position exactly and withholds its name. Two candidates have been argued for two centuries: Acquate, whose church forecourt is to this day the Sagrato don Abbondio, and Olate, argued by the Lecchese geologist Antonio Stoppani, who reconstructed the imagined village against the ground. We have pinned Olate, and the reason is the novel's own sightline: from the boat on the water the fugitives see Don Rodrigo's palace 'raised above the huts that crowded the base of the promontory', and Lucia picks out her own roof from the same water. Olate lies on the lake-facing flank of the Zucco; Acquate lies behind it, in the Caldone valley. The geometry works from one and not the other. Current Lecco sources still call the question unresolved, and they are right to.

THE INNOMINATO'S CASTLE contradicts its own author. Manzoni told Cesare Cantu that the character was Francesco Bernardino Visconti and that he had moved the castle 'into the Valsassina'. But the tradition since the first printed map of the Manzonian places, in 1830, puts it at the Rocca di Vercurago, and the novel's topography agrees: the torrent in the valley below is the state frontier, which ran exactly there; the cardinal's parish of Chiuso is 660 metres away; Don Rodrigo's house is 'not more than six miles' off. We have pinned the Rocca and left Manzoni's own sentence standing against it.

RENZO ENTERS PLAGUE-STRICKEN MILAN BY PORTA NUOVA, NOT PORTA ORIENTALE, and our own translation is the reason anyone thinks otherwise. Manzoni has him surface 'tra porta Orientale e porta Nuova, e molto vicino a questa' - between the two gates and much nearer the second. The 1834 translator flattened that to 'near the eastern gate', then contradicted himself a page later with 'the gate Nuova', which is where Renzo actually walks in. The two gates are 1.15 km apart and the whole of his walk across the dying city hangs off which one he used. The map follows Manzoni.

THE PLAGUE IS DRAWN AS THE THIRD CHARACTER, in the manner of Minard, and its band widens as the dying climbs - the inverse of the Grande Armee's, which narrows. Its path: the imperial army mustering at Lindau and passing Chur in May 1629, over the Alps to Chiavenna, into the Duchy at Colico in September, down the lake to Bellano, through the Valsassina to Lecco by 3 October; the protophysician Lodovico Settala reporting the first case in the territory to the Tribunal of Health on 20 October 1629; and Milan through 1630 to the Lazzaretto. Army strength 28,000 foot and 7,000 horse, with leave to cross in eight days; they took about twenty, plundering, which is the grievance Manzoni dramatises.

THE NUMBERS ARE MANZONI'S CHRONICLERS', AND THEY ARE ROUGHLY DOUBLE. He reports about 140,000 dead in a city of 200,000-250,000, following Ripamonti and Tadino. Modern work (Sella in the Storia di Milano; Alfani; Galli et al., iScience 2023) gives Milan about 130,000 people before the plague and about 60,000 dead across 1629-31 - catastrophic, and half what the chroniclers claimed. The map uses the modern figures.

THE PROCESSION DID NOT START IT. Both Ripamonti and Tadino blamed the procession of San Carlo's relics on 11 June 1630 for the surge that followed, and Manzoni lets the reader infer it. The 2023 reconstruction from the parish death registers finds that 67% of parishes had already recorded a plague death before that morning, and that 83% of the dying was still to come. Federigo Borromeo had resisted the procession on exactly these grounds and then yielded.

DATES: everything from chapter 19 to chapter 27 - the abduction, the castle, the conversion, the cardinal's visitation - is undated in the novel. Those days are interpolated between two fixed points: 13 November 1628, when the arrest order reaches the podesta of Lecco, and the army's descent in September 1629. Four deaths (Fra Cristoforo, Perpetua, Donna Prassede, Don Ferrante) are reported retrospectively and dated nowhere; each is placed with its uncertainty written on it.

Historical anchors: the tumulto di San Martino, 11-12 November 1628, is real, and the vicario di provvisione whose house the mob went for was Lodovico Melzi, who was awarded 300 gold scudi in compensation the following February. Antonio Ferrer, Grand Chancellor, really did carry him off in his own coach. Federigo Borromeo was Archbishop of Milan 1595-1631; his meeting with Visconti happened on a pastoral visit in 1619, nine years before the novel puts it.

regions.name: The lake, and the village that is never named

chapters.title: That branch of the Lake of Como
The notary and the two bailiffs
A night that would not end
Bread, and the price of it

characters.name: Renzo Tramaglino
characters.role: A silk-weaver of twenty, engaged to be married on the 8th of November 1628, and not married until the 11th of November 1630

characters.name: Lucia Mondella
characters.role: The bride, whose thread is the shorter of the two and the more helpless: she is moved by other people almost every time she moves at all

characters.name: Agnese
characters.role: Lucia's mother, who has the idea that starts the whole disaster and afterwards spends the book crossing and re-crossing the same twenty miles

characters.name: Fra Cristoforo
characters.role: A Capuchin who killed a man in his youth and has been apologising with his life ever since; the only person who confronts Don Rodrigo to his face

characters.name: Don Rodrigo
characters.role: The local lord, who makes a wager about a girl he has seen twice and destroys four lives to avoid losing it

characters.name: L'Innominato
characters.role: A man so feared that the novel will not give him a name, who takes delivery of Lucia and cannot go through with it

characters.name: The army, and the plague it carried
characters.role: Not a person: thirty-five thousand imperial troops crossing the Alps for the war over Mantua, and the pestilence that came down with them. Its band widens as the dying climbs

locations.name: Olate, above Lecco
locations.story: Renzo and Lucia's village, and the only place either of them wanted to be. Manzoni describes exactly where it stands and refuses to say what it is called - a refusal that has kept two Lecco parishes arguing for two hundred years.
locations.note: The novel never names it. Olate is Antonio Stoppani's identification and the one the sightline from the boat supports: from the water the fugitives see the palazzotto raised above the houses at the promontory's foot, which works from Olate's lake-facing slope and not from Acquate behind the hill. Acquate's rival claim is older and still live - its churchyard is called the Sagrato don Abbondio.
locations.quote: The bank, formed by the deposit of three large mountain streams, descends from the bases of two contiguous mountains, the one called St. Martin, the other by a Lombard name, Resegone, from its long line of summits, which in truth give it the appearance of a saw

locations.name: The parish church, Olate
locations.story: Where the wedding does not happen. Don Abbondio comes home along the lane where the two paths fork - the right hand climbing to the parsonage, the left going down to the torrent - and finds two men waiting at the little wayside chapel.
locations.note: The traditional Olate attribution: the church of the Santi Vitale e Valeria. San Giorgio at Acquate, whose forecourt is named for Don Abbondio, is the rival.
locations.quote: The inner walls of the two narrow paths, instead of meeting at the angle, ended in a little chapel, upon which were depicted certain long, sinuous, pointed shapes

locations.name: Don Rodrigo's palazzotto, the Zucco
locations.story: The house on the ridge that can see the whole village, which is the entire point of it. Fra Cristoforo is thrown out of its dining room; the bravoes go out of its gate at night; and from the boat it looks, Manzoni says, like a savage prowling over sleeping prey.
locations.note: The sixteenth-century Arrigoni villa on the Zucco above Olate, demolished in 1937 and built over. A minority tradition puts the palazzotto at Pomedo di Laorca instead.
locations.quote: the palace of Don Roderick, raised above the huts that crowded the base of the promontory, like a savage prowling in the dark over his slumbering prey.

locations.name: Lecco
locations.story: The town below, where you go for a lawyer and where the garrison is. Renzo walks down with four capons under his arm to buy justice from Doctor Azzeccagarbugli, and walks back up with the capons.
locations.note: 'Lecco, the largest of these villages, and which gives its name to the district' (ch. 1). The pin is the old market square.
locations.quote: Lecco, the largest of these villages, and which gives its name to the district, is situated at no great distance from the bridge, upon the margin of the lake

locations.name: The bridge at Lecco
locations.story: The hinge of the opening paragraph, and of the map: the exact place where the lake stops being a lake and goes back to being the Adda. Everything in this book happens within about fifty miles of it.
locations.note: The fourteenth-century Ponte Azzone Visconti. Manzoni marks it as the point where the lake ceases and the river recommences; the regiments are counted over it in 1629.
locations.quote: The bridge by which the two shores are here united, appears to render the transformation more apparent, and marks the point at which the lake ceases, and the Adda recommences

locations.name: The Capuchin convent, Pescarenico
locations.story: Fra Cristoforo's house, and the last safe place any of them touch. The three fugitives come down to the water's edge here at night; the friar puts them in a boat and never sees Lucia again.
locations.note: Manzoni notes the building 'still subsists'; the convent church of the Santi Materno e Lucia survives. He gives the hamlet as being on the left bank a few steps below the bridge.
locations.quote: Pescarenico is a small hamlet on the left bank of the Adda, or, rather, of the Lake, a few steps below the bridge; a group of houses, inhabited for the most part by fishermen, and adorned here and there with nets spread out to dry.

locations.name: Pescate
locations.novelName: the right bank of the Adda
locations.story: Where the boat puts them ashore in the dark, and where the carriage is waiting. Renzo, Lucia and Agnese part company two days later and do not stand in the same place again for twenty-two months.
locations.note: The novel gives only 'the right bank of the Adda' here, but names Pescate on the return journey in ch. 36, coming up from Monza - which fixes the landing.
locations.quote: as the bark carried them to the right bank of the Adda.

locations.name: Chiuso
locations.story: The parish the cardinal happens to be visiting on the night the Innominato cannot sleep. Lucia is brought down to a tailor's house here; her mother is fetched to her; and a rich, timid woman offers to take her to Milan.
locations.note: Manzoni suppresses the name in the novel but names Chiuso in his first draft, Fermo e Lucia, where the priest is 'the good priest of Chiuso' - Serafino Morazzone, whose house is now his museum. It is 660 metres from the Rocca.

locations.name: The Innominato's castle
locations.story: A castle above a valley on the summit of a cliff, where a man who is feared by governments discovers in one night that he cannot do this any more. Lucia spends a single night in it. Later half the valley shelters there from the German troops.
locations.note: The Rocca di Vercurago, identified with the castle since the first printed map of the Manzonian places in 1830. Manzoni himself wrote that he had moved Bernardino Visconti's castle 'into the Valsassina'; the novel's own topography - the frontier torrent in the valley, Chiuso just below - points here instead.
locations.quote: The castle of the Unknown was situated above a narrow and shady valley, on the summit of a cliff, which, belonging to a rugged chain of mountains, was nevertheless separated from them by banks, caverns, and precipices.

locations.name: Malanotte
locations.story: The tavern at the foot of the climb, where the carriage stops and the litter takes over. It had an inn sign with a rising sun painted on it, and everybody called it Bad Night anyway.
locations.note: A real cluster of houses below the Rocca; Via Malanotte at Calolziocorte carries the name. The tavern itself is not fixed to better than about a kilometre.
locations.quote: an old sign, with a rising sun painted on both sides, was suspended before the door; but the people gave the place the more appropriate name of Malanotte.

locations.name: Pasturo, in the Valsassina
locations.story: Where Agnese goes to sit out the plague among her relatives, on the grounds that it is not so bad up there. The imperial army had marched through Pasturo the previous autumn on its way down to Lecco.
locations.note: Named in the text twice, chs. 32 and 36. It also sits on the lansquenets' documented route through the Valsassina - the map draws both, and lets the reader notice.
locations.quote: She has gone to Valsassina, among her relatives at Pasturo; for they say that down there the pestilence has not made such ravages as it has here.

locations.name: Monza
locations.story: Where the carriage stops at sunrise and the family comes apart: Lucia and Agnese to the convent, Renzo on foot to Milan. He passes back through it twice more, once being handed bread with a pair of tongs.
locations.note: The inn is unnamed and unlocated; it is folded into this pin. Manzoni's own aside - 'which we believe to have been the name of the place' - is a joke about his manuscript source.
locations.quote: Our travellers arrived then at Monza, which we believe to have been the name of the place to which Father Christopher had directed Renzo, a little after sunrise.

locations.name: The convent of Santa Margherita, Monza
locations.story: Gertrude's convent, and the safest place they could think of. It is the least safe place in the book: the nun who takes Lucia in is being blackmailed, and hands her to the men who come for her.
locations.note: The novel never names the house. The historical monastery of Santa Margherita, where Marianna de Leyva was Sister Virginia, stood here; it was demolished around 1890 and its church survives on the piazza.

locations.name: Porta Orientale
locations.story: The gate Renzo walks in by on the day of the riot, past a long low building he is told is the lazaretto and does not look at twice. Two years later he goes out through it to look for Lucia in that building.
locations.note: The gate of the Spanish walls, on the line of the bastions at what is now Piazza Oberdan; renamed Porta Venezia in 1860. Not the medieval gate of the same name, which stood a kilometre inside it.
locations.quote: he followed the path which had been pointed out to him, and arrived at the eastern entrance, which consisted of two pilasters, with a roofing above to secure the gates, and on one side was a small house for the toll-gatherer.

locations.name: The bakery of the Crutches
locations.story: Where the bread riot starts, and where Renzo's whole life turns on being in a street. He arrives hungry in a city throwing flour into the road, picks up an opinion and a crowd, and is a wanted man by nightfall.
locations.note: Corsia de' Servi 16, now corso Vittorio Emanuele II between numbers 3 and 5, where a plaque stands; the bakery closed in 1919. The coordinate is interpolated to the Duomo end of the street and deserves a metre-level check.
locations.quote: In the street called the Corsia de' Servi there was, and is still, a bakery of the same name,—a name that signifies in Tuscan the Shop of the Crutches

locations.name: The square of the cathedral
locations.story: The bonfire of the bakers' tools, and the crossroads of both of Renzo's Milans: he passes through it in a mob on his first day, and alone through an empty plague city on his last.
locations.note: Piazza del Duomo. The cathedral was the landmark Renzo steered by across country - he takes its dome for his polar star.

locations.name: The house of the vicario di provvisione
locations.novelName: the house of the superintendent of provision
locations.story: The house the mob decides is responsible for the price of bread. Renzo makes a speech outside it and is marked down as a ringleader by a man who is listening. The Grand Chancellor arrives in his own coach and carries the vicario out through the crowd by flattering it.
locations.note: Manzoni names no street. The vicario in 1628 was Lodovico Melzi and the accounts of the tumult put his house near Santa Maria Segreta, just off the Cordusio. The fix is to the block, not the door. Melzi was awarded 300 gold scudi for the damage the following February.
locations.quote: Near by is the house of the superintendent of provision; let us do justice, and plunder it.

locations.name: The inn of the Full Moon
locations.novelName: a sign of the Full Moon
locations.story: Where a stranger buys Renzo his supper, gets him drunk, writes down his name, and has him arrested at dawn. He gets away in the street outside because the city is still too frightened of its own crowd to hold him.
locations.note: Manzoni gives no street - only that the tout led Renzo to it from the crowd near the Duomo. The pin is a short walk from the cathedral and is a guess.
locations.quote: And he entered a large gate, from which hung a sign of the Full Moon.

locations.name: Porta Nuova
locations.story: The gate Renzo actually enters the plague city by, having meant to try the first one he came to. A bastion hides it until he is almost through it. Inside there is a hand-barrow across the opening with a dying man on it.
locations.note: Our translation says he 'arrived before the walls of Milan near the eastern gate' and then contradicts itself. Manzoni puts him between the two gates and much nearer this one - 1.15 km from where the English implies. The Spanish gate stood well west of the medieval arch that now carries the name.
locations.quote: he proceeded, without being aware of it, to the gate Nuova, which had been hid from his view by a bastion, behind which it was then concealed.

locations.name: Don Ferrante's house
locations.story: Where Lucia spends twenty-two months being improved by a kind, insufferable woman, and where Renzo knocks two years later and is chased down the street as a plague-spreader for touching the wall.
locations.note: Manzoni names no street and no quarter for it. The pin is a placement, not a location, and is kept apart from Don Rodrigo's Milan house on principle: they must not be the same dot.

locations.name: Don Rodrigo's house in Milan
locations.story: Where he goes to be out of the cardinal's way and stays to be out of the plague's, until the morning he wakes with a swelling under his arm and finds that the one man he trusts has already gone for the monatti.
locations.note: 'A casa sua, in Milano' is the whole of what the novel gives. Pinned separately from Don Ferrante's house because the book keeps them separate.

locations.name: The Lazzaretto di San Gregorio
locations.story: A walled rectangle outside the eastern gate, three hundred and seventy metres by three hundred and seventy-eight, with two hundred and eighty-eight cells around a portico and a small octagonal church at the centre. In the summer of 1630 it held some sixteen thousand people. Every thread in this book ends up inside it.
locations.note: Demolished from 1882; the central chapel of San Carlo al Lazzaretto still stands on the spot and fixes the centre to within a few metres. Dimensions from Luca Beltrami's 1899 monograph, written from the survey made before demolition. The sixteen thousand is Tadino's count and Manzoni's figure; nobody has ever checked it.
locations.quote: in a little while you will find yourself by the side of a long and low building; that is the lazaretto; keep along the ditch that encircles it, and you will soon be at the eastern gate.

locations.name: Greco
locations.story: A hayloft on the last night of the walk south, close enough to Milan to see the dome in the morning. He has eaten nothing but two loaves handed to him at arm's length.
locations.note: Named in the text, ch. 32.
locations.quote: Towards evening he passed through Greco, and quitting the high road, went into the fields in search of some small house where he might pass the night

locations.name: Sesto San Giovanni
locations.story: Where the rain that ends the plague catches him on the way home, and does not stop.
locations.note: Named in the text, ch. 36.
locations.quote: He arrived at Sesto in the evening; the rain had as yet no appearance of ceasing.

locations.name: Gorgonzola
locations.story: A village inn where Renzo hears his own crime described by a traveller who was there, considerably improved, and understands for the first time that he cannot go home.
locations.note: Named in the text, ch. 16. He asks the host how far it is to the Adda and gets six miles.

locations.name: Trezzo sull'Adda
locations.story: Heard and never seen: a clock striking the half hours somewhere in the dark while Renzo is lost in a wood. It is the only thing in the novel that fixes where he crossed the river.
locations.note: Named in the text, ch. 17, as the probable source of the clock.
locations.quote: he heard, every half hour, in the deep silence, the heavy sound of some distant clock, probably that of Trezzo.

locations.name: The Adda below Trezzo
locations.story: The great scene of the first half: a man lost all night in a wood, hearing water and not daring to believe it, coming out on a bluff above the river at first light with another country on the far side.
locations.note: Manzoni names no crossing point and no scholar has fixed one. The clues are six miles from Gorgonzola, a cross-road to the left, heath and wood, a steep bluff - and the Adda runs in a gorge only in the Trezzo reach - Trezzo's clock, and Bergamo visible across the water. The pin is a reading of those, not a location.
locations.quote: He soon reached the extremity of the plain, and found himself on the edge of a steep precipice, whence looking downward, he discovered, through the bushes, the long-desired river, and, on the other side of it, villages scattered here and there, with hills in the distance

locations.name: Bortolo's village
locations.story: Where a cousin takes him in without asking questions, gives him a new name and a job in a silk-mill, and keeps him for two years while the warrant sits in a drawer in another country.
locations.note: Manzoni never names it and nobody has identified it. The only fix is his own arithmetic - nine miles from the landing and then two more, walking towards Bergamo, and short of the city. Low confidence, and said so.
locations.quote: at its entrance, he saw a very high house, with numerous windows, and perceived it to be a silk manufactory

locations.name: Bergamo
locations.story: The whitish mass on the hillside that Renzo sees across the water at dawn and walks towards for the rest of his life. The novel ends at a silk-mill near its gates.
locations.note: Venetian territory, and therefore out of reach of a Milanese warrant. Named repeatedly.
locations.quote: The master of another manufactory, situated near the gates of Bergamo, being dead, the inheritor of it, a young libertine, was willing to sell it half price, for ready money.

locations.name: Chur
locations.story: Where the army was on the 29th of May 1629, coming south for a war about who should inherit Mantua. Nobody in this book has heard of it.
locations.note: Documented staging point of the imperial column under Merode. The crossing of the Alps beyond it is inferred: Splugen and Septimer both funnel into Chiavenna and neither is named in an accessible source.

locations.name: Colico
locations.story: The first soil of the Duchy of Milan the troops set foot on, at the head of the lake, in September 1629.
locations.note: Named in the novel, ch. 28: 'Colico was the first territory of the duchy that these demons invaded'. The date is disputed between the 9th and the 20th of September.
locations.quote: Colico was the first territory of the duchy that these demons invaded; they then threw themselves on Bellano, from which they entered and spread themselves in the Valsassina, whence they marched into the territory of Lecco.

locations.name: Bellano
locations.story: The second place they came to, halfway down the lake. By early November fifty-nine people there were dead and three or four were dying every day.
locations.note: Named in the novel, ch. 28. The mortality is from the eyewitness account of Sigismondo Boldoni.

locations.name: Rimini
locations.story: Where Fra Cristoforo is sent to get him out of the way, on foot, the length of Italy, for the crime of having been right. He stays there until the plague gives him a reason to come back.
locations.note: Manzoni gives the whole journey one sentence: 'made to travel on foot from Pescarenico to Rimini'. Both of his long legs are drawn as gestures, because that is all the novel gives.
locations.quote: Friar Christopher was made to travel on foot from Pescarenico to Rimini, as we shall see.

locations.name: The Bergamask bank, towards Capriate
locations.novelName: the other side of the Adda
locations.story: Where the fisherman puts him ashore at first light, out of the Duchy of Milan and out of reach of it. He asks a passer-by whose country this is and is told: it is the territory of St Mark.
locations.note: The landing is as conjectured as the launching point opposite it; the novel gives a fisherman, a bark and the far bank, and no place-name at all.
locations.quote: It is the territory of St. Mark.

movements.routeNote: Down to the water at the mouth of the Bione in the dark, with the alarm bell going behind them.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 8: 'Now, go to the border of the lake, near the mouth of the Bione'.
movements.note: Out of the village they will not see again for two years

movements.routeNote: Across the water in a fishing boat, no wind, the lake smooth in the moonlight. Lucia turns round here and says goodbye to the mountains.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 8. The water is the Adda leaving the lake, which Manzoni establishes in his first paragraph.
movements.note: The most famous farewell in Italian, said with her back to where she is going

movements.routeNote: The old road out of the Lecco territory through the Brianza, in a cart, before dawn.
movements.routeSource: No route is named. This reconstructs the seventeenth-century Lecco-Monza road by Galbiate, Oggiono, Barzano and Missaglia.
movements.note: The last hours the three of them are together

movements.routeNote: A few hundred yards from the inn to the safest place anyone could think of.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 9.
movements.note: Into the care of a nun who is being blackmailed

movements.routeNote: Ten miles down the high road with a letter to a friar and no idea what he is walking into.
movements.routeSource: The novel gives the distance and the destination; the road is the Monza-Milan highway.
movements.note: He arrives on the second day of a bread riot

movements.routeNote: In at the gate past the lazaretto, and then the mob's own route, which Manzoni names turn by turn: the Grucce, Pescheria, the crooked arch, the square de' Mercanti, the Cordusio, and the house they have decided is to blame.
movements.routeSource: Chs. 11-12, bead by bead.
movements.note: He makes a speech he will be arrested for

movements.routeNote: A short walk with a stranger who has been listening and has offered to buy him supper.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 14. Neither the street nor the inn is located.
movements.note: The stranger writes his name down

movements.routeNote: Out through the square past yesterday's cold bonfire, out at the eastern gate, and then twelve miles of walking to get six miles from Milan, because he leaves the road whenever he sees anyone on it.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 16: 'To Bergamo? through the eastern gate. Take this street to the left'; and 'he had probably traversed twelve miles, when he was only six miles from Milan'.
movements.note: The first day of being a man with a warrant

movements.routeNote: Out at the Ave Maria, off to the left, and then lost all night in fern and broom with a clock striking somewhere he cannot see.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 17: six miles; a cross-road to the left; heath, wood, a bluff; a clock 'probably that of Trezzo'.
movements.note: The night he hears the river and does not dare believe it

movements.routeNote: A hundred and fifty metres of water, a fisherman, and another country on the far side.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 17. Neither bank is named; the reach is fixed by Trezzo's clock and the gorge.
movements.note: The frontier. On this side the warrant means nothing

movements.routeNote: Eleven miles towards the whitish mass on the hillside that is Bergamo.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 17: nine miles from the landing, and then two more.
movements.note: To a cousin who asks no questions and gives him a false name

movements.routeNote: Four hundred kilometres on foot, the length of Lombardy and down the Via Emilia, for having been right about a powerful man.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 19 gives the whole journey one sentence: 'made to travel on foot from Pescarenico to Rimini'. No stage is named, so the line is drawn as a gesture.
movements.note: Transferred, which is what the order calls it

movements.routeNote: North in a fishmonger's cart, leaving her daughter behind a grille she believes is the one safe thing in Lombardy.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 18: 'early in the morning they arrived at Pescarenico'.
movements.note: Home to an empty cottage

movements.routeNote: Six miles up the valley, equipped for the chase, to ask a favour of the one man more frightening than himself.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 19: 'The distance between his castle and that of Don Roderick was not more than six miles.'
movements.note: He has run out of people who will do this for him

movements.routeNote: Sent on an errand she was told was safe, taken at the corner by a carriage with the door open, and driven north-east for a whole day.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 21. The route is not given; this is the direct road from Monza to the Adda valley.
movements.note: The one journey in the book she does not take a single step of

movements.routeNote: Up the last of it in a litter, carried by men who will not look at her.
movements.note: To a castle nobody has ever come out of

movements.routeNote: Down the hill with a carbine on his shoulder to see a cardinal, having decided nothing.
movements.note: After the longest night in the book

movements.routeNote: Back up with a terrified parish priest beside him, to fetch a girl down.
movements.note: The hinge of the whole book, and it is one man changing his mind

movements.routeNote: Down again the next day in the same litter, with a good woman holding her hand and her mother on the way.
movements.note: Twelve hours, and the man who took her has changed his life

movements.routeNote: Home with his promise, and then out of the valley before sunrise, because a cardinal is in the parish asking questions.
movements.routeSource: Chs. 20 and 25. He leaves for Milan having risen before the sun; the road is the Lecco-Monza-Milan highway.
movements.note: Running away, and calling it business

movements.routeNote: To Milan with Donna Prassede, by way of her villa, to be improved.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 27. The villa is 'at some miles' distance' and nowhere located; the road is the Lecco-Monza-Milan highway.
movements.note: She will not move again for twenty-two months

movements.routeNote: Twenty-eight thousand foot and seven thousand horse over the Alps for a war about who should inherit Mantua. They had leave to cross the Duchy in eight days and took about twenty.
movements.routeSource: Documented at Chur on 29 May 1629 and quartered at Chiavenna through the summer. The pass itself is inferred: Splugen and Septimer both funnel into Chiavenna and no accessible source names which they used.
movements.note: Nobody in this book has heard of them yet

movements.routeNote: Down the eastern shore and through the Valsassina village by village, billeted on each in turn, into the territory of Lecco by the 3rd of October 1629.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 28 names Colico, Bellano, the Valsassina and the territory of Lecco in that order; the village-by-village passage is in the notarial records of Cortenova, Primaluna, Pasturo, Barzio, Cremeno and Moggio, and Cremeno billed the provisioning at 113 lire 19 soldi.
movements.note: The road Agnese will climb a year later to get away from what they left in it

movements.routeNote: Up to the castle of the man who took her daughter, because it is the one building the German troops will not enter.
movements.routeSource: Chs. 29-30. Half the territory shelters there and the Innominato feeds them all.
movements.note: The safest place in the valley is the one that terrified it

movements.routeNote: Home after three or four and twenty days, to a village the army has been through.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 30: 'Our fugitives remained three or four and twenty days in the castle'.
movements.note: The soldiers have gone. What they left has not

movements.routeNote: The army has gone on. From here the band is not men but deaths. On the 20th of October 1629 the protophysician Settala reported the contagion at Lecco, and then it went down the road all winter in the clothes of dead soldiers and on forged health passes.
movements.routeSource: Settala's report of 20 October 1629 to the Tribunal of Health; Manzoni names Chiuso in his first draft. Documented carriers include Geronimo Redaello, who left Merate on a forged licence on 22 November and was dead in Milan within two days.
movements.note: The first case anybody wrote down, and probably not the first

movements.routeNote: Up into the Valsassina to sit out the plague among relatives, on the grounds that it is not so bad up there.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 32: 'She has gone to Valsassina, among her relatives at Pasturo'.
movements.note: Up the road the army came down the previous autumn

movements.routeNote: It comes back on the 24th of March 1630 and is general in two-thirds of Milan's parishes by June.
movements.routeSource: Reconstructed from the parish death registers by Galli et al., iScience 2023.
movements.note: By the end of March the lazaretto held under three hundred people

movements.routeNote: The same four hundred kilometres back, at sixty, because the plague in Milan is the chance he has been waiting years for.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 34: 'He had not stirred from Rimini, and he would not now have thought of doing so if the plague breaking out at Milan had not afforded him the opportunity, so long desired, of sacrificing his life for the benefit of others.'
movements.note: He walks the length of Italy towards an epidemic on purpose

movements.routeNote: Eighty per cent of the dying falls between early June and the end of July 1630. About sixty thousand people die, out of about a hundred and thirty thousand.
movements.routeSource: The modern figures (Sella in the Storia di Milano; Alfani; Galli et al.). Manzoni, following Ripamonti and Tadino, gives roughly double.
movements.note: It ends where every thread in this book ends

movements.routeNote: Carried out of the house on a cart with the plague on her, in the same direction as everyone else in Milan.
movements.routeSource: Chs. 33-35. The novel does not narrate the journey, only that she was there and had recovered.
movements.note: She survives it. Don Ferrante and Donna Prassede do not

movements.routeNote: Carried out of his own house on a hand-barrow by the monatti, having been sold to them for his clothes by the servant he trusted most.
movements.note: The Griso takes the coat, and is dead of it within days

movements.routeNote: Back over the river to find out who is alive, taking the road to Lecco before venturing into Milan, and then south again through Monza where a shopkeeper hands him bread with a pair of tongs.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 32: 'He took the road to Lecco, before venturing into Milan', and the passage through Monza and Greco.
movements.note: Almost everyone he asks about is dead

via.name: the walls between the two gates

movements.routeNote: He comes out under the walls between Porta Orientale and Porta Nuova, much nearer the second, walks round a bastion that has been hiding it, and goes in there and across an emptied city to a door he has never seen.
movements.routeSource: Manzoni: 'tra porta Orientale e porta Nuova, e molto vicino a questa'. Our 1834 translation flattens this to 'near the eastern gate' and then corrects itself; the map follows the Italian. Ch. 33 names the street to the Naviglio, San Marco, the Borgo Nuovo and the Carrobio.
movements.note: The gate our own translation gets wrong

movements.routeNote: Chased through the streets as an untore, he saves himself by jumping onto a corpse-cart, and the monatti carry him out of the eastern gate.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 33. The mode is a compromise: the cart is neither a coach nor a walk, and he did not choose it.
movements.note: The worst ride in the book, and the one that saves him

movements.routeNote: Out into the rain that ends the plague, and forty miles home in it without stopping: Sesto, Monza, the flooded road, Pescate at dawn, the bridge, the fields.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 36: 'He reached Pescate; travelled along the Adda, giving a melancholy glance at Pescarenico; passed the bridge, and crossed the fields'.
movements.note: He has found her, and walks home through a thunderstorm without noticing

movements.routeNote: Down out of the mountains, fetched home by Renzo, with the hundred gold scudi still in their paper.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 36: 'he returned by the way of Pasturo, and conducted Agnes to her village home'.
movements.note: It is about to be a dowry

movements.routeNote: Home at last, after a quarantine in Milan the novel does not locate, one fine evening in a cart with the widow who nursed her.
movements.routeSource: Ch. 37: 'One fine evening Agnes heard a carriage drive up to the door of her cottage.'
movements.note: Two years and four days after she left

movements.routeNote: Married at last, and leaving: they sell everything and cross the river for good, to a silk mill near the gates of Bergamo going half price.
movements.note: Out of the country that would not let them marry

story.title: That branch of the Lake of Como
story.narration: Manzoni opens by telling you exactly where to stand: which arm of the lake, which headland, the bridge where the water stops being a lake and becomes the Adda again. He is the only author here who hands you the establishing shot in his first sentence.
story.quote: That branch of the Lake of Como, which turns toward the south between two unbroken chains of mountains, presenting to the eye a succession of bays and gulfs, formed by their jutting and retiring ridges, suddenly contracts itself between a headland to the right and an extended sloping bank on the left, and assumes the flow and appearance of a river.

story.title: Two men at the wayside chapel
story.narration: Towards evening on the 7th of November 1628 the curate of one of these villages finds two men waiting where the lane forks. They name a couple he is to marry tomorrow and tell him he is not to. The local lord has made a bet about the bride with his cousin.

story.title: The night of the deceits
story.narration: Fra Cristoforo has already been up to the great house to ask Don Rodrigo to behave, and been shown the door. So everyone tries at once, and every plan fails: an ambush marriage in the curate's parlour, bravoes at an empty cottage, and a sexton who rings the alarm bell and panics the kidnappers.

presenceOk.cristoforo: Named for a visit he made earlier the same day; he is back at Pescarenico by nightfall.
presenceOk.rodrigo: Named as the man who ordered it. He is at his own house and sends the bravoes.

story.title: Down to the water
story.narration: The bell is still going behind them. The friar has a boat waiting at the mouth of the Bione, and the three of them go down through the dark to the lake.

story.title: Farewell, ye mountains
story.narration: No wind, the lake smooth in the moonlight, the only sound the oars. Lucia sits with her back to where she is going and says goodbye to a skyline, in the most famous paragraph in Italian. On the map it is a camera turning round.
story.quote: Farewell, ye mountains, source of waters! farewell to your varied summits, familiar as the faces of friends! ye torrents, whose voices have been heard from infancy! Farewell!

story.title: A little after sunrise
story.narration: A cart on the old road through the Brianza. Here the book divides: she goes to a convent, he goes on to Milan with a letter, and the map carries two separate threads for the next twenty-two months.

story.title: The safest place they could think of
story.narration: The convent of the signora, who receives Lucia kindly. The signora was put here at fourteen by her father, has a lover, and is being blackmailed by him. She is why Lucia will be handed to the men who come.

story.title: And him, to Milan
story.narration: We leave Lucia behind a grille. Renzo walks the last ten miles alone with a letter to a friar, expecting a bed and some advice.

story.title: Into Milan
story.narration: In at the eastern gate, past a long low building he is told is the lazaretto and does not look at twice. He walks into a city on the second day of a bread riot, with loaves in the street and flour trodden into the road.

story.title: The mob's own route
story.narration: Manzoni names every turn and the map follows it: the ransacked bakery of the Crutches, the bonfire of the bakers' tools, Pescheria, the crooked arch, the square de' Mercanti, the Cordusio, and the house of the official they have decided is to blame. Renzo makes a speech about justice and a man writes his name down.

story.title: The Full Moon
story.narration: The Grand Chancellor has just carried the official out of the riot under his own carriage seat by flattering the crowd. A friendly stranger buys Renzo his supper, keeps his glass filled, gets his name and his village, and leaves.

story.title: Out, and twelve miles to go six
story.narration: Bailiffs at dawn, and he gets away in the street by shouting that they are taking an honest man, which in Milan that week is all it takes. Then he leaves the road whenever he sees anybody on it, and walks twelve miles to get six miles out.

story.title: It is the Adda
story.narration: At the inn he hears a traveller describe the Milan riot, and the dangerous ringleader in the story is him. He leaves at the Ave Maria and is lost all night in fern and broom, until the wind brings him a sound he does not dare believe.
story.quote: the wind brought a new sound to his ear—the murmur of running water. Intently listening, to ascertain if his senses did not deceive him, he cried out, "It is the Adda!"

story.title: The territory of St Mark
story.narration: A hundred and fifty metres of water, a fisherman who asks nothing, and another state on the far side. The whole second half hangs on this: on that bank a Milanese warrant is a piece of paper.

story.title: The country of his adoption
story.narration: Eleven miles towards the whitish mass on the hillside that is Bergamo. His cousin takes him in, asks nothing, and gives him a job and a false name.

story.title: Four hundred kilometres, on foot
story.narration: The order comes and the friar is sent to Rimini: the length of Lombardy and down the Via Emilia, on foot, at his age, for having told Don Rodrigo in his own doorway that a day would come. Manzoni gives the journey one sentence, so the map draws one gesture and says so.

presenceOk.rodrigo: Named in a recollection of the doorway scene. He is not on the road to Rimini.

story.title: Meanwhile
story.narration: While the friar walks south, the clock goes back three weeks and the other thread picks up in Monza.

story.title: Agnese goes home
story.narration: She leaves her daughter behind a convent grille, which she believes is the one safe place in Lombardy, and rides north in a fishmonger's cart to an empty cottage.

story.title: Six miles up the valley
story.narration: He has run out of people who will do this for him. Equipped for the chase, with an escort, Don Rodrigo rides up to ask a favour of a man so far outside the law that governments negotiate with him, and whose name the novel will not print.

story.title: The carriage at the corner
story.narration: The signora sends her on a short errand outside the walls, having been told to. A carriage is waiting with the door open. It is the one journey in the novel Lucia does not take a single step of.

story.title: Up to the castle
story.narration: The carriage stops at a tavern below the climb that everybody calls Bad Night, and a litter takes her the rest of the way, carried by men who will not look at her.

story.title: The longest night in the book
story.narration: Upstairs she promises the Virgin she will never marry if she is got out of this, and means it. Downstairs the man who has her cannot sleep, and Manzoni gives him a night of it: everything he has ever done, arriving in order, and the pistols on the wall. In the morning he hears bells.

story.title: Down to the cardinal
story.narration: He rides down with a carbine on his shoulder, having decided nothing, and is received by Federigo Borromeo with an embrace and a question about what he has come for. He finds an answer while being asked.

story.title: Back up with a curate
story.narration: He rides up again with the parish priest beside him on a mule, terrified out of his wits, to fetch a girl down. The hinge of the whole novel is not a battle. It is one man changing his mind and acting on it the same afternoon.

story.title: She comes down
story.narration: The same litter, the same road, twelve hours later. A good woman is waiting with clothes and a fire, her mother is on the way, and a hundred gold scudi arrive in a paper that nobody knows how to refuse.

story.title: Donna Prassede takes her
story.narration: A rich, kind, entirely insufferable woman decides Lucia needs saving from her own attachment and takes her to Milan to be improved. Lucia goes because refusing would be ungrateful, and will not move again for twenty-two months.

story.title: Out of the valley before sunrise
story.narration: He goes home with his promise, and then discovers urgent business in Milan, because a cardinal is in the parish taking names. He calls it business. The map draws it as what it is.

story.title: Something else on the map
story.narration: Nobody here has heard of the war over Mantua, and it is about to decide all their lives. This thread is not a person: it is thirty-five thousand imperial troops, and what came down with them. Minard's rule - the width is the number of people. Napoleon's band narrows. This one widens.

story.title: Over the Alps
story.narration: They were at Chur at the end of May 1629 and quartered at Chiavenna all summer. They had leave to cross the Duchy of Milan in eight days and took about twenty, living off it as they went.

story.title: Down the lake, and through the Valsassina
story.narration: Colico first, then Bellano, then village by village up the valley, billeted on each in turn with the notaries writing down what it cost. By the 3rd of October 1629 they were in Lecco, and being counted over the bridge the first paragraph pointed at.

story.title: Meanwhile
story.narration: Back four days, to the valley the troops are walking into, and the people in it.

story.title: Everyone goes up the hill
story.narration: Half the valley takes to the castle, because the one building the German troops will not enter is the one that used to terrify them. Agnese shelters for three or four and twenty days in the house her daughter was a prisoner in, and is fed by the man who took her.

presenceOk.contagion: The contagion is not a person and cannot be present or absent: by 1630 it is everywhere in the frame. The thread is drawn as a band, not as somebody who arrives.

story.title: The twentieth of October
story.narration: The army has gone. From here the band is not men but deaths. On the 20th of October 1629 the protophysician Settala reported the contagion at Lecco - the first case anyone wrote down, and probably not the first. Then it went down the road all winter, in the clothes of dead soldiers and on forged health passes.

story.title: Meanwhile
story.narration: Back again, out of the contagion for a moment: the village had a war to get through first.

story.title: Home to what they left
story.narration: The soldiers have gone on towards Mantua. The village is standing. What is in it now is not.

story.title: It comes back in March
story.narration: The epidemic resumes on the 24th of March 1630 and is general in two-thirds of Milan's parishes by June. Both of Manzoni's sources blamed the procession of San Carlo's relics on the 11th of June for what followed. The parish registers say the city was already burning when it went looking for a match.

story.title: Meanwhile
story.narration: Back to the early summer of 1630, and a man in Rimini who has waited two years for a reason to come north.

story.title: And four hundred back
story.narration: He has not stirred from Rimini. Then the plague breaks out in Milan and gives him the thing he has wanted since he killed a man in a street: somewhere to spend himself. He walks the length of Italy towards an epidemic on purpose.

presenceOk.contagion: The contagion is not a person and cannot be present or absent: by 1630 it is everywhere in the frame. The thread is drawn as a band, not as somebody who arrives.

story.title: Sixteen thousand
story.narration: Eighty per cent of the dying falls between June and the end of July 1630. Manzoni's chroniclers give about a hundred and forty thousand dead. The registers give a city of a hundred and thirty thousand and sixty thousand dead - half his figure, and still one person in two.
story.quote: The reader may imagine the lazaretto, peopled with sixteen thousand persons infected with the plague: the vast enclosure was encumbered with cabins, tents, cars, and human beings.

story.title: Meanwhile
story.narration: Back to the spring, and the one person here whose plan worked.

story.title: Up to the Valsassina
story.narration: Agnese goes to relatives at Pasturo, on the grounds that the pestilence has not made such ravages up there. She walks up the road the army came down.

story.title: She is carried out too
story.narration: Donna Prassede is dead and Don Ferrante is dead, and Lucia is carried out of the house on a cart in the same direction as everybody else in Milan. Manzoni does not narrate the journey. He simply has her be there, later, alive.

story.title: Onto the cart
story.narration: Chased through the streets as a plague-spreader by people who mean to tear him apart, he saves his life by jumping onto a passing cart of corpses, and the monatti carry him out through the eastern gate, laughing.

story.title: Meanwhile
story.narration: Back six days. Before Renzo reaches Milan, the man who started all this is carried out of his own house.

story.title: The Griso fetches the monatti
story.narration: Late in August 1630 Don Rodrigo wakes with a swelling under his arm. The one servant he trusts goes out for a doctor and comes back with the corpse-carriers and a price. They carry him off; the Griso takes his coat, and is dead of it within days.

story.title: Three days after
story.narration: Renzo has had the plague and recovered, which in 1630 is a passport. He comes back over the river to find out who is alive; almost everyone he asks about is dead. Then south through Monza, where a shopkeeper hands him bread with a pair of tongs.

presenceOk.contagion: The contagion is not a person and cannot be present or absent: by 1630 it is everywhere in the frame. The thread is drawn as a band, not as somebody who arrives.

story.title: The gate Nuova
story.narration: He comes out under the walls between the two gates, much nearer the northern one, and walks round a bastion that has been hiding it. Then across an emptied city to a door he has never seen. A voice says she is at the lazaretto.

presenceOk.contagion: The contagion is not a person and cannot be present or absent: by 1630 it is everywhere in the frame. The thread is drawn as a band, not as somebody who arrives.

story.title: Whom he found there
story.narration: Fourteen hectares and sixteen thousand people. He finds Fra Cristoforo first, dying and still working, who releases him from what he came in carrying by walking him to a hut where Don Rodrigo lies insensible. Then he finds Lucia, well, and bound by her vow.

story.title: The rain
story.narration: The rain that ends the plague starts as he walks out of the gate and does not stop. Sesto, Monza, the flooded road, Pescate at first light, a glance across at Pescarenico, the bridge, the fields. Forty miles in a thunderstorm, and he barely notices he is wet.

presenceOk.contagion: The contagion is not a person and cannot be present or absent: by 1630 it is everywhere in the frame. The thread is drawn as a band, not as somebody who arrives.

story.title: Down out of the mountains
story.narration: He goes up into the Valsassina for her mother and they come home together, with the hundred gold scudi still in their paper. It is about to be a dowry.

presenceOk.contagion: The contagion is not a person and cannot be present or absent: by 1630 it is everywhere in the frame. The thread is drawn as a band, not as somebody who arrives.

story.title: One fine evening
story.narration: Her quarantine over, Lucia comes home in a cart with the widow who nursed her, one fine evening in the middle of October 1630. Agnese hears the wheels at her own door. It is two years and four days since the three of them went down to the boat.

presenceOk.contagion: The contagion is not a person and cannot be present or absent: by 1630 it is everywhere in the frame. The thread is drawn as a band, not as somebody who arrives.

story.title: Over the river for good
story.narration: The vow is dissolved on the ground that a frightened girl had no right to promise away what was not only hers; Don Abbondio, who started all this by being afraid, marries them at last. Then they sell up and cross the Adda, to a silk mill near the gates of Bergamo going half price.

presenceOk.contagion: The contagion is not a person and cannot be present or absent: by 1630 it is everywhere in the frame. The thread is drawn as a band, not as somebody who arrives.

story.title: And that is the whole of it
story.narration: All of it happened within fifty miles of the bridge the first sentence pointed at, bar one friar's walk to Rimini and one army's from the Alps. Manzoni framed the shot, then proved a place that small can hold a bread riot, a state frontier, a private army and sixty thousand deaths.

presenceOk.contagion: The contagion is not a person and cannot be present or absent: by 1630 it is everywhere in the frame. The thread is drawn as a band, not as somebody who arrives.
